doctrine.statement: Gen 2:7 uses לְ of what the man became: God formed him of dust and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, "and the man became a living soul". The soul is what the formed and breathing man came to be, not a thing put into him; the same "living soul" is said of the beasts (Gen 1:24). Paul keeps the Hebrew construction, "the first man Adam became (ἐγένετο εἰς) a living soul", and sets against it "the last Adam became a life-giving spirit" (1Co 15:45). So man as made is a living, mortal creature, and the life beyond the grave is given through the last Adam, not carried in a soul from the first.

Leviticus 23 sets the appointed times down with לְ two ways: each is "to Yahweh" (a sabbath לַיהוָה, Lev 23:3; a passover לַיהוָה, Lev 23:5), and each is "to you", a holy convocation and a sabbath of rest לָכֶם (Lev 23:7, 32). They are Yahweh's own ("these are my appointed times", Lev 23:2), and given for his people's good: "Yahweh has given you the sabbath" (Exo 16:29). Jesus says the same of the sabbath: "the sabbath was made for man, not man for the sabbath" (Mrk 2:27).

gloss: (preposition) to, for; belonging to, of; into, as; according to; (with an infinitive) to, in order to
note: Root investigation (2026-11-13). No root is viable; the entry is keyed by its own consonant ל, as min is keyed מנ. (1) The particle is one consonant with a short vowel in every language that has it (Hebrew lə-, Aramaic and Syriac l-, Ugaritic l /li-/, Phoenician l-, Sabaic l-, Ge'ez la-, Arabic li-/la-), and with suffixes it is built on that letter alone (לוֹ, לָכֶם; Ugaritic lh, lkm; Arabic lahu, lakum), with no third-weak base such as עַל (עָלָיו, from עלה) and אֶל (אֵלָיו) show. So nothing in its form points to a longer root. (2) The verb לָוָה "join, attach" (Gen 29:34; Num 18:2, 4; Isa 56:3, 6) has a sense near "belonging to", but no cognate dictionary derives l- from lwy and the suffixed forms show no w or y: rejected. (3) אֶל: kept apart. Hebrew, Phoenician and Arabic each have both words side by side with different ranges (Phoenician l- "never of direction", Krahmalkov p. 248; Arabic li- and ʾilā); אֶל has a longer y-base and לְ none; and Ugaritic has l but no ʾl "to". אֶל is a word of the elah entry (root אלה), not of el-al (which holds the negative אַל, root אלל); nothing here proposes moving it. (4) Akkadian has no l- preposition (ana, ina); Segert's "Akkad. < Aram. la" is a late loan from Aramaic and is not cited. Amorite la (Segert p. 190) is noted only. Not checked: Dillmann for Ge'ez ለ (only Wiktionary cited); Payne Smith for Syriac ܠ (SEDRA only); CAL for Aramaic. Left out: the conditional לוּ (l.ar.aa, in lo.json), the emphatic or vocative la- some see in Hebrew, and the compounds BDB files elsewhere: לִפְנֵי (panah), לְמַעַן (under ענה), לָכֵן (l.bp.ag, "see כֵּן"), לָמָּה (מָה). The Hebrew letter's own BDB key l.aa.aa ("twelfth letter") is not claimed. Token counts: the corpus links no token to l.aa.ab. OSHB tags every suffixed form (לִי, לוֹ, לְךָ, לָהֶם …, about 4,500 tokens, and about 60 in the Aramaic) with the bare lemma "l" and no Strong's number, and the generator's build_surface_entries only links lemmas with a number, so lexicon-support will show no uses for לְ or its Aramaic until that is fixed. The prefixed לְ is a proclitic counted under the word it joins, as with מִן. The senses are illustrated, not exhaustive.
summary: The preposition of the one or the thing a matter is directed to: the person spoken to or given to ("I am giving to you", Lev 23:10), the one it is for or belongs to ("a holy convocation shall be to you", Lev 23:7; "the earth is Yahweh's", Psa 24:1), what a thing becomes ("the man became a living soul", Gen 2:7), the measure it goes by ("after its kind"), a time it is set at, and, before an infinitive, the purpose of an act ("to seek out a resting place for them", Num 10:33). It is always joined to the next word (לְ־, לַ־, לִ־) and takes suffixes straight on its single letter: לִי, לְךָ, לוֹ, לָנוּ, לָכֶם, לָהֶם, and poetic לָמוֹ. The same one-letter word is in every branch of the family (Ugaritic, Phoenician, Aramaic, Syriac, Arabic, Sabaic, Ge'ez), but no noun or verb is known for it to have grown from, so it is keyed by its own consonant; it is not the same word as אֶל "to, toward", which stands beside it in Hebrew, Phoenician and Arabic with a different range and a longer base.

senses.definition: The place a movement goes to, and the person speech or a call is directed to.

evidence.note: "Abraham returned לִמְקֹמוֹ, to his place."
"וּלְאָדָם אָמַר, and to Adam he said."
In מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ, “Who told you?”, לְךָ identifies the hearer and the following כִּי clause gives the message.
"Moses said לְחֹבָב, to Hobab"; in the same verse the people go אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם "to the place": direction of travel takes אֶל, the one addressed takes לְ.

In מַה יִּקְרָא לוֹ, “what would he call it?”, לוֹ marks each creature to which the man gives a name. The verse closes with הוּא שְׁמוֹ, “that was its name.”

"וּלְקַחְתֶּם לָכֶם, you shall take for yourselves" the fruit of goodly trees.
The Aramaic: "לָךְ, to you, God of my fathers, I give thanks … you have given לִי, to me, wisdom and might."
The Aramaic: "לָךְ, to you, God of my fathers, I give thanks … you have given לִי, to me, wisdom."

words.summary: Never written alone: it is prefixed (לְמִינוֹ, Gen 1:11), takes the article's vowel (לַחֹדֶשׁ, Lev 23:5; לַיהוָה, Lev 23:3), and with suffixes is built straight on the one letter, לִי "to me", לְךָ "to you", לוֹ "to him", לָנוּ "to us" (Num 10:31), לָכֶם "to you" (Lev 23:7 and through the chapter), לָהֶם "to them" (Num 10:33), as Ugaritic ly, lk, lh, lkm, lhm and Arabic lī, lahu, lakum, lahum, with no longer base such as אֶל has (אֵלָיו). Its senses all start from one picture, the one or the thing a matter is directed to or set down for, and it covers what Greek does with the dative case: to whom something is said or given, for whom it is done, whose it is. The database counts none of its tokens under this word yet (see the entry's note).

words.summary: A longer form of לְ with an added -mô, found only in Job (27:14; 29:21; 38:40; 40:4); the same ending makes the poetic suffixed לָמוֹ "to them" (Psa 2:4; Deu 32:35). Ugaritic has the same lengthened lm beside l.

senses.definition: Before a noun, the object of a verb; before an infinitive, its purpose.

words.summary: Scripture's Aramaic has the same preposition with the same range, and uses it much more often than Hebrew to mark a verb's object (Dan 2:12), as Ugaritic and especially Syriac do. With suffixes: לָךְ, לִי (Dan 2:23), לְכוֹן (Dan 3:4), לְהֹם.
